title: The Deposition Across the River
body: Word comes to camp at dusk: the one witness in the Bhagwanpura poisoning — an old man who saw the sweets handed over — is dying at his village across the nullah, and asking for the sahib. A deposition taken tonight convicts; a deposition not taken dies with him before morning. The nullah is up after unseasonable rain, mud-brown and pulling, and the guide, asked if the ford is passable, gives the answer guides give: doubtless, sahib, if God is willing. Your horse does not like the water. Horses are seldom wrong about water.

choices.label: Ford it tonight, deposition papers and all.

risk.outcome: The ford was deeper than the guide swore and the current older than his family's memory of it. The horse goes over, you go under, and the deposition forms go down the nullah to the sea. A constable pulls you out a furlong down, minus a boot, plus the beginnings of a fever that will keep its own calendar. The witness dies at dawn, unrecorded. The sub-division hears the whole story by Tuesday, improved.

choices.outcome: Wet to the armpits, swearing in two languages, you get over with the forms held above your head like regimental colours. The deposition is taken by lantern; the old man tells it clearly, signs his thumb, and dies contented at having discomposed his enemies. The conviction follows in due course. The tahsildar, hearing how it was got, says nothing and re-tells it for a year.

choices.label: Wait for first light and pray he lasts.
choices.outcome: Prudence, the manuals agree, is a virtue. The nullah is down by dawn and the crossing easy, and the old man is an hour dead when you reach the village, and the case dies in the file marked ‘evidence insufficient.’ The poisoner prospers modestly ever after. On certain evenings you will remember that the guide said doubtless, and that you heard the doubt and took it.

choices.label: Send the sub-inspector over alone; it is his district too.
choices.outcome: He goes because he is told to, and gets over because he is luckier than you deserve, and takes a deposition that a defence pleader will later pick apart because no magistrate witnessed it. Half a conviction, at no risk to yourself. The sub-inspector never mentions it. His report does, in the passive voice, where such things are kept.

title: The Thakur's Leopard
body: A cattle-lifting leopard has set up in the ravines below Rajgarh, and the Thakur organises a beat with the flourish of a man staging a durbar: elephants borrowed, beaters in his livery, luncheon under a shamiana. The first drive wounds the beast — a bad shot, not yours — and it goes into a cane-brake trailing blood. Every man present knows the etiquette: a wounded leopard is followed up on foot by somebody, and the somebody who does it is talked of, and the somebody who declines is also talked of. The Thakur looks at you with bright, hospitable, merciless interest.

choices.label: Take the shotgun and go into the cane after it.

risk.outcome: It comes from the left, low and silent, which is how they come. You are aware of a weight, a smell of hot copper, a noise you discover later was your own gun going off against its chest — and then men shouting, and sky. Forty stitches at the mission hospital, a scar from shoulder to elbow, and a story that will buy your dinners for thirty years. The Civil Surgeon, sewing, observes that the district is hard enough on probationers without their volunteering.

choices.outcome: Twenty yards of cane, a heartbeat of yellow, and one barrel at a range where missing is not among the outcomes. It is over before fear has finished forming. You walk out carrying your gun wrongly and trying not to shake, and the beaters put their hands to their foreheads, and the Thakur is embracing, expansive, delighted — a young sahib after his own heart. The story reaches headquarters before you do.

choices.label: Let the Thakur's shikari earn his salt; it is his trade.
choices.outcome: The shikari goes in with a borrowed rifle and thirty years of knowing better, and finishes it neatly, and is given twenty rupees and no dinner-table immortality whatever. It is the sensible course and everyone says so, in the tone the Service keeps for sensible courses. The Thakur's warmth cools by a calculated degree. At the Club, the story is told without your name in it.

choices.label: Declare the light gone and the beat over; leopards keep.
choices.outcome: A wounded cattle-lifter left in cover is a debt at interest, and the sub-division pays it: a herd-boy mauled at Rajgarh a fortnight on, not fatally, but talked of. The Thakur has the beast destroyed his own way, with nets and spears and no sahibs invited. The invitation list of the district quietly re-forms itself around your absence.

title: The Grey That Killed a Subaltern
body: The cantonment side is a man short for the cold-weather polo, and the man they are short of is you, and the pony they can lend you is the grey — fast as telegrams, beautifully schooled, and famous for having put a subaltern of the Guides into the cemetery two seasons back by falling on him at the turn. The soldiers are perfectly frank about all of it, which is their way of asking whether Civilians can ride. The alternative mount is a hireling with a mouth like a cab-horse and the turning circle of a barge.

choices.label: Take the grey, and play it like a gentleman in a hurry.

risk.outcome: At the second chukker's turn the grey props, changes its mind, changes it back, and comes down — on the leg, mercifully, and not the head, which is the margin between a story and a headstone. A crack, a whiteness, the polished boots of the entire cantonment arriving at a run. Six weeks of splints and the Civil Surgeon's conversation. The soldiers send fruit, and put you down — you learn much later — as game, which was rather the object, though not by this route.

choices.outcome: The grey goes like the mail and turns like a rumour, and you sit it — just — and hit one goal off a scramble that was mostly the pony's idea. The cantonment revises its view of Civilians by one honest inch, which along this frontier of the two Services is a treaty. You dine in mess after, and are made to sing, and the cold weather is suddenly a very good one.

choices.label: Take the hireling and play safe, ugly polo.
choices.outcome: You block, and hook, and trundle, and are exactly as useful as a gate. The side loses respectably; nobody is buried. A major observes, passing the tea-tent, that the Civil arm rides with great discretion, and the word does the little rounds it was minted for. Still — you played, which counts for something on both sides of the mall.

choices.label: Plead the assizes; the Service before sport.
choices.outcome: The excuse is real — the file exists, the work is done, the virtue solid — and it purchases nothing whatever. The cantonment wanted to see the new Civilian ride, and has instead seen him decline to, and along the mall that is a complete set of facts. The assizes, at least, are beautifully prepared.

title: The Pleader Who Collects Magistrates
body: Babu Brindaban Chatterji, B.A., has practised in Kotra longer than you have been alive, and collects young magistrates as other men collect moths. Today, mid-case, he begins: a citation you half-know, a High Court ruling you don't, a courteous request that the Court instruct him — the Court being so lately from England — on a point the Court manifestly cannot answer. The tahsildar's face has become porcelain. The whole cutcherry waits to see the pin go through the specimen.

choices.label: Admit ignorance from the bench, and adjourn to read the ruling.
choices.outcome: ‘The Court is obliged to the learned pleader, has not read the ruling, and will have done so by Thursday.’ A stir; porcelain cracking into something like respect. By Thursday you have read it twice and it does not say what he implied it says, and you tell him so with the page numbers. Brindaban bows very low — the bow he keeps, the tahsildar explains later, for magistrates who cannot be collected.

choices.label: Bluff through it on tone; the bench must never wobble.
choices.outcome: You rule with confidence, wrongly, and Brindaban thanks the Court with a purring completeness that tells the whole room he has what he came for. The appeal, when it succeeds at the district, cites your ruling in full. The Collector returns it to you without a note, which is the loudest thing he does all season.

choices.label: Fine him for trifling with the Court's time.
choices.outcome: Ten rupees, paid with a bow of infinite gratitude — you have made him, for the price of a dinner, the martyr of the district bar. Three pleaders reproduce the performance within the month, fines and all, the fee for the advertisement being now established. The bench holds firm and the bar dines out on it.

consult.opinion: Bishan Lal murmurs behind the register. ‘Fine him, Huzoor. Ten rupees, and the district sees the bench has teeth; the younger pleaders will think twice.’ He guards the Court’s dignity as if it were his own, which it is. But Brindaban has paid larger fines for smaller advertisements, and wears each one to the next young magistrate like a campaign medal.

title: The Mail Cart Robbed at the Stones
body: The dak cart is stopped at the standing stones two miles short of Kotra — runner tied to a milestone, insured parcels gone, and with them the tahsil's registered remittance and the sub-division's official post. Robbing the mail is not theft, the police manual observes; it is an act against Government, and sub-divisions are judged by whether it can happen twice. The sub-inspector has a theory, a favourite informer, and a face that wants very much to be told to go and be vigorous somewhere.

choices.label: Saturate the roads: pickets, searches, the whole apparatus.
choices.outcome: For a fortnight no cart moves at night without a lantern and a challenge, and honest carters are searched with the rest and say so, bitterly. The gang lies quiet, then tries the Pipalgaon road, and is taken at a picket by a constable who will dine on it for a decade. The mail is not robbed twice. The roads remember the searches, too.

choices.label: Work the informer, quietly, and wait for the fence to move.
choices.outcome: The informer earns his dirty little retainer: the parcels surface in a grain-pit at Pipalgaon, the fence names the gang with the aggrieved thoroughness of a man cheated of his share, and the arrests are made at dinner, undramatically, which is how the best arrests go. The manual would have preferred more marching. The result column does not say so.

choices.label: Report it up and let the district police own the case.
choices.outcome: It is, technically, correct. A district superintendent arrives with his own theory and his own informers, obliterates the local scent in a week of energy, and departs leaving the case open and the impression — carefully worded in his diary — that Kotra's young civilian prefers his robberies handled by post. The gang robs the Tuesday cart in April, as if to sign the verdict.

title: One Well Between Two Villages
body: Mauza Rampur and mauza Shahpur share a boundary, a bitter history, and — since Shahpur's well went brackish in October — one sweet well between them. Rampur has begun charging for what it calls courtesy; Shahpur has begun arriving at the well in numbers that make courtesy unnecessary; and last market-day there were lathis out under the banyan, which is one step short of the step nobody comes back from. Both headmen are before your camp table, each with witnesses, genealogies, and a version of 1857.

choices.label: Sink Government's own well at Shahpur, and be done.
choices.outcome: The sanction takes three reminders and the boring crew arrive scandalously late, but by the hot weather Shahpur draws its own sweet water and the banyan shade returns to gossip and small litigation. The district office queries the expenditure in red ink. You answer with the thana's nil return for the quarter, and hear no more of it.

choices.label: Fix a water-turn by written order: hours, buckets, and a chaprassi to watch.
choices.outcome: The order is beautiful, laminated in office varnish, and obeyed to the letter — the letter being the point, since each village now files monthly petitions alleging violations of sub-clause three. The chaprassi at the well becomes the best-informed man in the pargana. Peace of a kind holds: paper peace, renewable quarterly, at your table.

choices.label: Tell them sternly to settle it as neighbours, and ride on.
choices.outcome: They settle it as neighbours: at the next full moon, with lathis, seven broken heads, and a case that fills your file for a month and the pleaders' pockets for two. The sub-inspector's report does not say ‘the sahib was told,’ because sub-inspectors do not write such sentences. The tahsildar's silence says it fluently.

consult.opinion: The Tahsildar has an opinion and no hesitation. ‘The record is the record, Huzoor. Divide the well against it to please two villages and every man with a grievance and a cousin in the office will want his own case reopened before the rains.’ He is thinking of his collections, which is his work — and which, this once, is also the law.

title: Smallpox at Pipalgaon
body: Two children dead at Pipalgaon and the marks on them beyond argument: smallpox, in the hot weather, with the fair a month out. The vaccinator — one man, one pony, one box of lymph going bad in the heat — has been driven from the village twice; the word has gone round that the needle is a Government mark to count souls for a new tax, and the priest of the smallpox goddess does not discourage the theory, arithmetic at the shrine being what it is. The Civil Surgeon's note is one line: contain it now or name the fair after it.

choices.label: Go yourself, and be vaccinated again in the village square.
choices.outcome: You sit on a string cot before the whole of Pipalgaon and take the needle, and the tahsildar takes it after you, and then the headman's wife — who has buried one of the two children and is done with theories — brings her remaining three. After that it is a queue. The lymph holds, the fair is held, the goddess's priest reports a satisfactory season regardless. The Civil Surgeon's next note is two lines, and one of them is nearly warm.

choices.label: Vaccinate the fair-roads by order, with police at the vaccinator's back.
choices.outcome: It is done, at the pace of a picket line, thoroughly and sullenly. The outbreak dies before the fair; the story of the needles and the constables does not, and reaches your file two years hence, transmuted, the next time Government wants anything at Pipalgaon. Epidemiology will count it a victory. The village books it under a different head.

choices.label: Quarantine the village and let it burn out inside its bounds.
choices.outcome: The cordon holds because you feed it and the village does not starve because you feed that too, and eleven more die inside the line, none of whom needed to. The fair is saved, the figures defensible, the method a hundred years old. The vaccinator, disbanded roadside, asks the tahsildar what the lymph was for. There is no answer in the file.

title: The Man Who Bought the Bazaar
body: Prices have climbed all through the heat, and now the reason has a name: Motilal, grain-dealer of Kotra, has quietly bought forward the whole of three tahsils' surplus and shut his godowns to watch the figure rise. There is no law against it, and nothing even unusual in it; only the poorer bazaar is down to one meal, the constable on the grain-market beat reports the quiet he does not like, and Motilal, calling to pay his respects, mentions how warmly he subscribed to the Christmas fund.

choices.label: Break the corner: force his godowns open for sale at a fixed price.

risk.outcome: The godowns open at your order and the bazaar, seeing the doors go back, decides the grain is Government's gift and therefore already its own. Ten minutes of surge, a broken gate, two constables down and a woman trampled at the second door before the line holds. The corner is broken; so is the market's temper for a season. The enquiry finds your order lawful and your arrangements thin, and both findings are correct.

choices.outcome: You post the order at the kotwali and stand a magistrate's presence in the market while it is executed, and the grain comes out at a price the poor can pay and Motilal can survive. He takes it, in the long view, well enough: Government has shown him its edge, and a dealer values a Government with an edge, the same being creditworthy. The bazaar eats that night, and knows why.

choices.label: Summon him privately and suggest the corner might unwind.
choices.outcome: Tea, compliments, twenty minutes of the weather, and then one sentence about godowns and the temper of hot-weather crowds, left where he can see it. Motilal, no fool, sells down over a fortnight at a profit merely handsome. The bazaar never knows the corner existed, which is the measure of the job done properly — and the reason no report of it can ever be written.

choices.label: The market is the market; Government does not fix prices.
choices.outcome: It is sound doctrine and you hold to it while the bazaar thins its meals to the edge of the possible. The rains break the corner in the end, as rains do, and Motilal banks the difference. What the doctrine cost is not in any return: only the constable on the grain beat could total it, and he keeps his totals to himself.

title: An Error in the Thakur's Favour
body: Checking the settlement maps against the patwari's field-book — the munshi's drill, now habit — you find it: forty acres of the best riverain land entered under the Thakur of Rajgarh that the survey of 1881 shows under three cultivators of mauza Bhagwanpura. A pen's width on the map; three families' bread in the field. The error is old, the Thakur's pleader will call it settled, the patwari who made it is dead, and the Thakur has lately been so very hospitable with his leopards and his luncheons.

choices.label: Correct the record and restore the land, whatever it costs at Rajgarh.

ifTrue.outcome: The correction goes through and the Thakur receives it with exquisite courtesy and total comprehension: the mare, the luncheons, the beat — all invested, all lost. His pleader files the appeal by return dak; his hospitality turns off like a tap; and word runs the district that the young sahib cannot be obliged, which costs you dinners and buys you something the dinners were pricing. The three families take their land back quietly, as men do who never expected justice and are unsure of its warranty.

ifFalse.outcome: The correction goes through; the appeal follows; the appeal fails, the field-book being unanswerable. Forty acres of riverain go back to three households who had farmed them as tenants of their own land for twenty years. The Thakur is cold at the next durbar, and the district notes the coldness, and notes too that the maps in Kotra now mean what they say. A settlement officer's dry postscript: ‘error regretted; correction confirmed.’

choices.label: Let sleeping surveys lie; reopen nothing.
choices.outcome: The field-book goes back to its shelf and the map stays authoritative and wrong. The Thakur's luncheons continue. The three families of Bhagwanpura continue also — as tenants, paying rent on their grandfather's land to a man whose title is a clerk's slip. You do not check the maps against the field-book quite so often after that.

choices.label: Refer it to the Collector with the papers and no recommendation.
choices.outcome: The file goes up beautifully arranged and perfectly neutral, and comes back in a month with one line in red: Correct the record. Why was a recommendation not made? The land is restored, the Thakur is cold at you anyway — the file bears your signature — and you have taught the Collector something about you that you will spend two seasons unteaching.

title: The Quarrel Above Your Head
body: The Canal Engineer and the District Superintendent of Police have not spoken since the incident with the snipe-jheel and the shooting lease — the facts of which have long been overtaken by the annotations — and Kotra’s tiny station society has divided into two dinner-tables accordingly. You are junior to both, useful to both, and this week both have invited you for Saturday. There is no Saturday with two dinners in it. The Club steward, who has watched twenty years of this, polishes glasses with the detachment of a man watching weather form.

choices.label: Dine with neither: invent a camp inspection and sleep in a tent.
choices.outcome: The tent is real, the inspection nearly, and the sub-division profits by a boundary case heard at dawn that would otherwise have waited a month. Both tables note the dodge and neither can fault it; a probationer at his work is unanswerable. It cannot be done every Saturday; it is a very good trick once.

choices.label: Dine with both: soup and fish at one table, joint and savoury at the other.
choices.outcome: It requires a synchronised khitmutgar, a bicycle, and nerve, and it succeeds so completely that both principals discover it the same evening and are forced — each having half a dinner's worth of grievance — to laugh. They laugh at you together, which is the first thing they have done together since the jheel. The reconciliation does not quite follow, but the tables merge for Christmas, and the steward gives you the look he reserves for promising material.

choices.label: Accept the senior man's table and post the junior a graceful regret.
choices.outcome: Correct, safe, and scored to a nicety: the Engineer's table gains a junior, the Superintendent's list gains a name in the margin. Policemen keep margins long after engineers have forgotten dinners. You will meet that margin again in some file about lock-up returns, wearing procedural clothes, and you will not quite be able to prove where it was born.

title: The Padre's School
body: The Reverend Mr. Elphick of the American Mission — twenty years at Kotra, dusty, indestructible, loved and priced accurately by everyone — wants the sahib's name at the head of his new school subscription, and a Government grant besides. The school is real and good and teaches sweepers' children their letters, which is the trouble: the bania quarter has no wish to fund the education of its future clerks' competitors, and the orthodox have petitioned against Government money touching a mission at all. Mr. Elphick sits before you, hat on knee, with the patience of a man who has outlasted seven of you.

choices.label: Head the list, move the grant, and let the petitions come.
choices.outcome: The grant goes through against a headwind of paper, and your name at the head of the list is quoted in three petitions as proof of Government's designs upon religion. The school opens with forty pupils and a portrait of the Queen-Empress. Years on, a copying-clerk in some collectorate will write a fair hand because of it; nobody will trace the hand to you, which is, Mr. Elphick would say, rather the point of the exercise.

choices.label: Subscribe privately; Government's name stays off mission paper.
choices.outcome: Fifty rupees under a plain initial, and the official file closed with a minute so balanced it could stand on its edge. Mr. Elphick pockets the cheque and reads the minute and smiles like leather creasing: he has seen this compromise seven times too. The school opens smaller. The orthodox claim the victory; the bania quarter claims the economy; the sweepers' children divide what is left.

choices.label: Decline both: the Service is neutral in matters of religion.
choices.outcome: The doctrine is unimpeachable and you deliver it well, and Mr. Elphick hears it out with his head tilted like a man listening to rain on a roof he has already mended. He builds the school anyway, two years slower, on Ohio money. Neutrality is preserved. What it was neutral between, the sweeper quarter could tell you, but nobody files their returns.

title: The Travelling Pillar
body: Boundary pillar XLIV, which fixes the line between two estates and incidentally between two irrigation rights, has moved. Not fallen: moved — eleven feet west, replanted with care, whitewashed fresher than its brothers. Both zamindars express astonishment. The patwari's memory has failed with a completeness that suggests instruction. Eleven feet west is worth perhaps forty rupees of water a year; men have gone to the sessions over four annas. The pillar stands in the winter wheat looking as innocent as anything in masonry can.

choices.label: Re-fix it by theodolite from the survey marks, publicly, with both parties present.
choices.outcome: A morning of chains and angles before a gallery of forty, the instrument glinting like justice, and the pillar goes back east eleven feet to the inch, watched by both zamindars with faces of civic satisfaction over private arithmetic. Nobody is charged; everybody is warned; the pargana grasps that the marks in the record can be conjured back out of it at will. Pillars keep still for years after such a morning.

choices.label: Prosecute someone for mischief; pillars do not walk unaided.
choices.outcome: The case is good until it meets the witnesses, all of whom saw nothing on a moonless night arranged for the purpose. It dies of failed memory in your own court, having cost two hearings and made the patwari an enemy with a long ledger. The pillar, meanwhile, stays where the mischief put it until the survey can be paid to travel. Prosecution was the correct instinct and the wrong tool, a distinction the cold weather is teaching you weekly.

choices.label: Note it for the next settlement; eleven feet can wait its turn.
choices.outcome: The note is accurate and the queue is long, and by the time the settlement party arrives — two years, as it proves — pillar XLIV has moved twice more and bred a suit, a counter-suit, and one first-class affray. Water arithmetic does not wait its turn. It compounds, like the interest at Sohan Lal's, and some other magistrate collects the sum.

title: The Thakur's Entertainment
body: The Thakur's cold-weather entertainment is the event of the pargana: fireworks, a banquet in two cuisines, and afterwards — the point of the evening, not printed on the card — a nautch, with singers down from Lucknow whose names mean nothing to you and a great deal to everyone else. The older Service went to nautches as it went to durbars; the newer opinion, with the Padre and the ladies behind it, calls them what the mission tracts call them. The Collector, consulted by telegram, replies with maddening serenity: USE YOUR JUDGMENT.

choices.label: Attend the whole evening, nautch and all, as the old Service did.
choices.outcome: The singing is the finest thing you have heard in India and you say so, and the Thakur glows, and every landholder present marks that the sahib sat it out like a guest and not an inspector. The pargana's doors open an inch wider ever after. At the station, the Padre's sister develops a way of not seeing you at the Club that will last until Easter, and your name comes off two dinner lists by Christmas.

choices.label: Dine, toast, and withdraw before the singers — the diplomatic hour.
choices.outcome: You leave on the last of the fireworks with compliments so rounded the Thakur cannot find the edge of them, and your tonga is heard leaving by exactly the people who needed to hear it. Both worlds are half-satisfied, which the Service, on the whole, counts a full success. The munshi, asked next morning how the singing had been, permits himself: ‘Sahib, it was the singing of Lucknow.’ You will always slightly wonder.

choices.label: Decline the card altogether; a magistrate is not entertained by suitors.
choices.outcome: It is the purest reading of the rules, and the Thakur receives your regrets with a courtesy that drops the local temperature two degrees for a season. Half his suits are before your file, so the scruple is real; the pargana merely notes that the new sahib holds himself apart, and deals with you thereafter at arm's length, papers first. Clean hands, cold company. It is a trade, like everything out here.

consult.opinion: The Secretary sets down his peg. ‘My dear fellow, dine, toast, and come away before the singers. The Padre’s sister keeps a list, and a young man’s name once entered on it stays entered. Lucknow nautch-girls will not confirm you; the station will.’ Half the Thakur’s suits are on your file, and the Thakur remembers a tonga that left early.

title: The Copying-Clerk's Cough
body: Hari Ram, second copying-clerk, has been dying quietly at his table all through the heat — the cough, the wrists, the beautiful unwavering hand — and everyone in the office knows it, and the office has arranged itself around not saying so, since his pay feeds eleven people and a pension wants five more years of service he does not have. Today he faints across the criminal register, and the question he has been keeping off your table falls onto it: the establishment rules on one side, eleven people on the other, and the hot weather auditing everyone impartially.

choices.label: Sick-leave on full pay, on your own responsibility, and hang the audit.
choices.outcome: Three months at his village under the mango trees, pay drawn as if present — a fiction your office maintains with the solidarity of a regiment. The audit query arrives in September, and you answer it with a candour that makes the Deputy Auditor read it twice. Hari Ram dies in the cold weather, at home, under the mango trees, his son taken on as third clerk the same week.

choices.label: Invalid him by the book, with the gratuity the rules allow.
choices.outcome: The medical board sits, the certificate signs him out, the gratuity is three hundred and twelve rupees and audit-proof. It is everything the rules provide and the rules provide little; eleven people learn to live on a third of what they lived on. The office accepts it as offices accept weather. The register he fainted on keeps a small tea-coloured stain under the sessions entries, which you find yourself not sending for rebinding.

choices.label: Keep him at his table lightly loaded; work is a kind of medicine.
choices.outcome: It is kindly meant and he is grateful, and he dies at the table in August with the pen in his hand, half through a mutation entry — which spares the pension question and answers the others. The office says only that he was a great copyist. The file he did not finish goes to the third clerk, who completes it in a hand nearly as beautiful, having been taught by his father.

title: The Collector's Dog Defects
body: The Collector's fox-terrier, Binks — a personage of the district, mentioned in demi-official correspondence — has taken to walking the two miles to your bungalow and installing himself on your verandah with the air of an inspecting officer. Nothing recalls him: not the orderly sent for the purpose, not dignity, not dinner. The Collector's note on the subject is a masterpiece of the man: Keep him till he bores of you. He is an excellent judge of juniors, and has never once been wrong in reverse. Binks stays a fortnight, reviews your household, and departs as he came. You find you miss him disproportionately.

title: The Dust-Devil in the Compound
body: At the dead hour a dust-devil comes off the maidan and walks through the compound like a slow brown djinn: forty feet of spinning grit that takes the office's entire out-tray, ascends it in a spiral of pending correspondence, and distributes the sub-division's business over three villages and a tank. The chaprassis pursue official paper through the cactus with lathis. A goatherd returns form XIV (Cattle Pound, Monthly) the next morning, gravely, asking whether there is a reward. You pay him from your own pocket and enter the afternoon, in the office diary, as dust-storm; correspondence delayed — the driest sentence you will ever write about the day the sky read your files.

title: The Crowd in the Grain-Market
body: A rumour of short weights, a shopkeeper’s shutter down, and now three hundred men in the lane between the thana and the temple, in a temper the Sub-Inspector cannot read. ‘An order, Huzoor,’ he keeps saying, as if the word itself were a plan. You have twenty constables and no Collector within forty miles.

choices.label: Clear the lane with the reserve, at once.
choices.outcome: The constables go in with lathis up — and the lane does not clear. It folds back on itself and hardens, and a brick comes over the wall and takes a man beside you across the ear. The temper has found its shape now, and the shape is facing you.

then.title: The Lane Will Not Clear
then.body: Twenty men against three hundred in a street a bullock-cart would block. Behind you the thana; ahead, the thing you have made. The Sub-Inspector has his hand on his revolver and his eyes on you, waiting to be told something he can put in a report.

choices.label: Order the charge home and take the street.
choices.outcome: It is done as it is always done: the line goes in hard, the street clears in bloody minutes, and by dark the town is silent and sullen and yours. Three men are in hospital and one will not leave it. The report writes itself; the reading of it, at the durbar and in the vernacular press, will take a year.

choices.label: Pull the police back inside and hold the thana.
choices.outcome: You give up the street rather than pay for it, and the crowd has its afternoon of ownership — a shutter or two broken, a great deal of shouting, and by evening the tide goes out of its own accord, as tides do. Nobody is in hospital. Everybody, from the Sub-Inspector to the Commissioner, has noted that the Sahib blinked.

choices.label: Go out in front of them, alone, and ask what they want.
choices.outcome: You walk out past the last constable into the open lane, alone, and the sheer unexpectedness of it buys the thirty seconds in which a crowd decides what it is. You ask the front rank, by name where you know them, what the trouble is; and it is, of course, the weights. You promise the scales checked by morning, and mean it, and the thing comes apart into three hundred men going home to their dinner.

risk.outcome: You walk out alone, and the crowd does not pause to be charmed. A press, a surge, a stick you never see — and the constables drag you back through the thana door with your puggree gone and your arm hanging wrong. It is a fortnight in bed and a great deal longer in the telling: the boy who mistook a mob for a deputation.

choices.label: Send for the headmen and the aggrieved shopkeeper both; hold the lane with talk.
choices.outcome: You do the slow thing: the headmen fetched, the shopkeeper produced, the offending scales sent for and weighed in front of the front rank. It takes two hours and a deal of standing about in the sun, and it works, which the quick thing might not have. The Sub-Inspector is disappointed. He had wanted an order.

choices.label: Bolt the thana and wait the temper out.
choices.outcome: You wait, which is not nothing — a crowd is a fire, and fires go out — but you wait behind a locked door, and the town notes the door. By evening the lane is empty, the shutters are up, and the weights are exactly as crooked as they were. You have kept the peace by declining to govern, which is a thing a man may do once.

title: The Gang at Khairi
body: The sub-inspector rides in before breakfast with news three days old and a face that has been hoarding it: Bhikan Singh’s gang — four dacoities and a spearing since the rains — is lying up at Khairi, fed by half the village and married into the other half. He wants an order to go in and take them, and he wants it in writing, and he wants it now, before word of his own arrival outruns the word he has brought.

choices.label: Send the police in tonight to ring the village and take them.
choices.outcome: You give the order and the sub-inspector goes off gladdened. By the time the cordon closes at midnight the village has known for two hours — a boy on a fast pony, a fire lit on a roof — and Bhikan Singh is away into the standing cane behind the houses with his men and his notice served. A constable comes back at dawn to report the lane barred with carts and the headman deaf to all summons.

then.title: The Lane Is Barred
then.body: You ride out to Khairi in the grey light. The lane is stopped with two bullock-carts and forty men behind them, sullen and unarmed and immovable; the gang is long into the cane and everyone knows it; and the sub-inspector, cheated of his dacoits, has fixed on the headman as the next best thing and wants him taken for harbouring. The whole village waits to see whether the sahib has come for justice or for a face to carry home.

choices.label: Arrest the headman for harbouring, and be seen to do something.
choices.outcome: He comes quietly, which is worse than if he had fought: a grey old man walked out of his own lane past his own people for a crime the whole village shares and he chiefly did not. The case wilts in your court inside the month, every witness gone conveniently deaf. Khairi remembers the arrest long after it has forgotten the gang, and the next dacoit finds the village readier to hide him, not less.

choices.label: Leave the headman his liberty, and put a price on Bhikan Singh instead.
choices.outcome: You let the old man keep his lane and post on Bhikan Singh a reward larger than his gang’s loyalty and payable in a coin the cane cannot spend. It takes six weeks. He is given up in the end by his own cousin, quietly, for the money and an old grudge. Four dacoities out of five end so, whatever the sub-inspector believes of his cordons.

choices.label: Send the constables back and sit down in the lane to talk.
choices.outcome: You wave the police off a hundred paces, sit on a cart-shaft, and ask the front rank without a notebook why a decent village shelters a spearman. It is a long morning, and the answer when it comes is a land quarrel, a marriage, and a fear of the gang worse than any fear of you. The headman rolls back a cart himself. Bhikan Singh you take later; Khairi you keep for good.

choices.label: Work the informer first; take them on the road, not in the village.
choices.outcome: You hold the sub-inspector back and set his informer to earn his retainer, and a fortnight on the gang is taken on the Pipalgaon road with the loot still in the cart, undramatically and well clear of anyone’s cousins. Khairi is never entered at all, and never forgets that it was spared.

choices.label: Refer it up to the district superintendent; a standing gang is his affair.
choices.outcome: It is correct, and it is slow. The superintendent arrives in ten days with a plan and a camp, by which time Bhikan Singh has moved two tahsils on, and the file records that Kotra declined to act on its own information. The sub-inspector says nothing. His diary says it for him, in the passive voice.

title: The Bond That Was Never Signed
body: Girdhari, a cultivator of Bhagwanpura with the face of a man who has not slept, lays a bond before you: his thumb-mark, his father’s land pledged against a debt he swears he never took, held by Lala Ram Sahai, the biggest money in three villages. The seal is good, the witnesses respectable, the stamp regular. Only Girdhari says the sum was four hundred and the paper reads four thousand, and that he set his thumb to a blank. It is the commonest fraud in the district and the hardest to prove, and Ram Sahai has never once been made to prove anything.

choices.label: Take the case up yourself and summon Ram Sahai to answer.
choices.outcome: You issue the summons over your own signature, a thing that has not happened to Ram Sahai in the memory of his gumashta. He comes, unhurried, with a pleader and two respectable witnesses and an air of wounded patience. And on the second hearing Girdhari’s own brother-in-law, who was to swear to the blank thumb-mark, sends word that he remembers nothing and is unwell.

then.title: The Witness Falls Ill
then.body: The case is coming apart in the accustomed way: the one honest witness gone deaf and feverish overnight, the bond standing unshaken, Girdhari’s courage draining as he watches the machinery he set going swing round to face him. Ram Sahai’s pleader, all silk, lets fall in the corridor that his client, from pure benevolence, would take the four hundred and tear the paper — were the case withdrawn today, before the Court is troubled further.

choices.label: Send the bond to Calcutta for a handwriting and stamp examination.

risk.outcome: The examiner reports what examiners report when the forgery is a good one: the stamp genuine, the seal genuine, the thumb-mark Girdhari’s beyond dispute. That was never the question, and it settles nothing. The case dies for want of the one thing paper cannot show. Ram Sahai withdraws his benevolence and the four hundred with it, and forecloses at leisure; Girdhari’s land changes hands in the spring.

choices.outcome: The Calcutta expert takes six weeks and finds it: the body of the bond laid down in a later ink than the signature line, over a thumb-mark set to a blank, exactly as Girdhari swore. Ram Sahai’s respectable witnesses discover pressing business elsewhere. The prosecution does not quite convict him — such men are not quite convicted — but the bond is void, the land is safe, and the biggest money in three villages has been made, once, to answer for a paper.

choices.label: Take the settlement: four hundred paid, the bond torn, the case withdrawn.
choices.outcome: You call both men in and the thing is done in ten minutes: the four thousand shrinks to four hundred, the paper is torn across before your eyes, and Girdhari keeps his land and a gratitude that is painful to sit through. Ram Sahai bows himself out uncharged and uncontrite, having bought a magistrate’s court off for the price of his own first loan. He will cut the next blank bond a shade more carefully.

choices.label: Press on to judgment on Girdhari’s word alone, witness or none.
choices.outcome: You believe Girdhari, and you are right to, and belief is not evidence. Without the brother-in-law the bond stands unrebutted, and a magistrate who decrees against a registered instrument on a debtor’s bare oath is a magistrate whose decree will not outlive the first appeal. It does not. The district reverses you, the land goes to Ram Sahai with costs, and being right is charged to Girdhari’s account, not to yours.

choices.label: Refer him to a civil suit; a disputed bond is matter for the civil court.
choices.outcome: It is the correct pigeon-hole and you place him in it: a civil suit, court fees he cannot raise, two years he does not have, against a man who breakfasts on litigation. Girdhari folds his hands and goes, and the land is Ram Sahai’s by the next harvest, wholly in order and wholly according to law. Your file is clean. So, now, is the Lala’s title.

choices.label: Warn Ram Sahai off quietly, without a case at all.
choices.outcome: You send for the Lala and mention, over no record whatever, that the bond has been noticed and would not bear a close reading. He hears you out with perfect deference and alters nothing that can be seen; the foreclosure merely turns slow and considerate, and arrives at the same door by a gentler road. A word off the record binds a man who fears the record. Ram Sahai fears nothing that is not written down.
